content: MT-TT, also referred to as Mitochondrially Encoded tRNA Threonine, is a transfer RNA molecule encoded by the mitochondrial MT-TT gene in humans. The MT-TT gene is located on the p arm of mitochondrial DNA at position 12 and spans 66 base pairs. Structurally, tRNA molecules exhibit a unique folded configuration characterized by three hairpin loops, resembling a three-leafed clover. MT-TT is a small RNA molecule consisting of 66 nucleotides (mapped to human mitochondrial DNA positions 15888–15953). Its primary function is to transfer the amino acid threonine to a growing polypeptide chain at the ribosome during protein synthesis, a process known as translation. Mutations in the MT-TT gene have been associated with Myoclonic Epilepsy with Ragged-Red Fibers (MERRF), a mitochondrial disorder that leads to deficiencies in mitochondrial energy production and reduced oxidative phosphorylation. MERRF is a rare condition that affects multiple systems in the body, particularly the muscles and nervous system. Symptoms of MERRF typically manifest during childhood or adolescence and vary significantly among affected individuals, even within the same family. Common clinical features include myoclonus, myopathy, spasticity, epilepsy, peripheral neuropathy, dementia, ataxia, and muscle atrophy. Additionally, MT-TT mutations have been linked to lethal infantile mitochondrial myopathy, Parkinson's disease (associated with the 15950G>A mutation), and an unconfirmed heart disease linked to the 15923A>G mutation. MT-TT mutations can also result in cytochrome c oxidase deficiency, a condition characterized by a defect in complex IV of the mitochondrial respiratory chain. This rare genetic disorder can affect various tissues, including skeletal muscles, the heart, the brain, and the liver. Clinical manifestations of cytochrome c oxidase deficiency include myopathy, hypotonia, encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. A specific mutation, 15915G>A, has been identified in a patient with cytochrome c oxidase deficiency, presenting with seizures, progressive hearing loss, and muscle weakness.
